title: Flight Bearing Calculator: Route Headings
description: Get the initial great-circle heading for a flight leg with the Flight Bearing Calculator — the course a long-haul route starts on. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, JFK to Heathrow starts on a heading of approx. 051° — northeast — although the destination sits across an ocean most people picture as 'straight east'.
quick_answer: The Flight Bearing Calculator gives the initial great-circle heading between two airports or places — the course the shortest flight path starts on. Because the Earth curves, that heading is often far from the direction the destination appears to lie on a flat map, especially on long east–west legs.

body.t: Students building a great-circle plan leg by leg start each leg with its initial bearing. This calculator is the quick check against the manual formula.
“Why are we flying toward Iceland to reach New York?” ends with the initial bearing and a globe. The number — 288° out of Heathrow — makes the curved route rational.
Flight-sim pilots planning long hauls use real initial bearings to fly believable oceanic tracks instead of the sim's straight ruler lines.
When a GPS leg course looks wrong, an independent spherical calculation from the same coordinates is the fastest referee — see also the
JFK → Heathrow: initial bearing approx. 51.4°. Return, Heathrow → JFK: approx. 287.9°. Two headings, neither the reverse of the other — the signature of great-circle flight over a curved ocean.

JFK → LAX starts at approx. 273.8° — a few degrees north of due west — and the heading keeps bending south-west as the route progresses. The initial bearing is a starting instruction, not the whole story.

popular_table.intro: Initial great-circle bearings between major airports from published coordinates — approx. values, reproducible for any pair in the tool.
popular_table.note: Bearings are initial only: a great-circle heading changes continuously, which is why oceanic flights are planned as a chain of waypoint legs.

faq: Is the flight bearing the same as the course flown?
It is the starting course of the great-circle path. Real flights fly airways and organised track systems that approximate the great circle, so the flown headings step around this value leg by leg.
Why is the bearing to a place not toward it on my map?
Your map is a projection; the bearing is computed on the sphere. For long east–west legs the shortest path genuinely departs toward the pole side of the ruler line.
True, measured from geographic north. Cockpit compasses read magnetic; the conversion depends on local variation and the aircraft's systems handle it — study plans should note the distinction.
Can I use cities instead of airports?
Yes — any two points work. Airport coordinates are simply the natural inputs for flight legs, and the Airport Distance Calculator shares them.
Wind changes the heading needed to hold a course, not the course itself. This tool computes the geometric course; drift correction is a separate, in-flight calculation.
How is this different from the Bearing Calculator?
Same spherical mathematics, flight framing: airports as inputs, legs as the unit of thought, and examples drawn from real route pairs.
What about the bearing halfway along?
It differs from the initial bearing — that continuous change is the defining property of great-circle sailing and flying, and why the word 'initial' is in the tool's family name.
